extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of literature (especially African/postcolonial studies)
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biography summarising Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's life, works, literary positions, and influence; serves as a reference for readers, students, and researchers of African and postcolonial literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in native African languages / advocate native-language literature
rubrics_metrics.description: “wrote primarily in English before switching to writing primarily in Gikuyu and becoming a strong advocate for literature written in native African languages.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context and rationale in the page: Decolonising the Mind argues for African writers' expression in their native languages rather than European languages “in order to renounce lingering colonial ties and to build authentic African literature.” Examples: Ngũgĩ founded and edited the Gikuyu-language journal Mũtĩiri; wrote the first modern novel in Gikuyu (Devil on the Cross); later works (e.g., The Perfect Nine) were originally in Gikuyu. Implication: privileging native-language composition/transmission is presented as a criterion for cultural authenticity and decolonisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should encourage spontaneity and audience participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ “sought to liberate the theatrical process from what he held to be 'the general bourgeois education system', by encouraging spontaneity and audience participation in the performances.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding explanation: his project aimed to 'demystify' the theatrical process and to avoid the 'process of alienation [that] produces a gallery of active stars and an undifferentiated mass of grateful admirers' which, he argued, encourages passivity in 'ordinary people'. Example: the community theatre project in Kamiriithu and the play Ngaahika Ndeenda; practical consequence: productions prioritising participation and demystification may be politically contentious (Ngaahika Ndeenda was shut down by the regime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical 'alienation' and star-focused performance
rubrics_metrics.description: He sought to 'demystify' the theatrical process and to avoid the 'process of alienation [that] produces a gallery of active stars and an undifferentiated mass of grateful admirers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an anti-pattern: conventional theatre that elevates stars and creates a passive audience is to be resisted. Guidance implied: design performances that distribute agency, engage communities, and resist spectacle-as-domination. Example: Kamiriithu Community Education and Cultural Centre's emphasis on community theatre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre African literature and oral traditions in teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: He argued that after the end of colonialism, it was imperative that a university in Africa teach African literature, including oral literature, and that such should be done with the realization of the richness of African languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical outcome noted: while at the University of Nairobi his efforts contributed to dropping English Literature as the central course and replacing it with a programme positioning African literature (oral and written) at the centre. Implication for curriculum design: prioritise indigenous literatures and oral forms rather than inherited colonial curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literature as political and social critique (anti-colonial engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ's works include essays and fiction that condemn colonialism and elites and carry strong political messages; e.g., Petals of Blood and Ngaahika Ndeenda provoked government repression, and his political writing led to imprisonment and exile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page frames political engagement as a defining characteristic and possible consequence of such writing. Examples: confiscation of books, arrest and detention, writing a prison novel on toilet paper (Devil on the Cross). Implied evaluative standard: works that confront injustice and colonial legacies are artistically and socially significant but may be risky under repressive regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate and disseminate work to reach broader linguistic communities
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2016 short story 'The Upright Revolution: Or Why Humans Walk Upright' "has been translated into more than 100 languages" and was released in projects aiming to translate stories into thousands of African languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page presents wide translation as a strategy for broad cultural impact and accessibility; Ngũgĩ also translated some of his own work (e.g., Wizard of the Crow translated to English by the author). Example: Jalada Africa Trust translation issue and the project's ambition to translate into 2,000 African languages. Implication: translation (including self-translation) is a tool for circulation and cross-cultural reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate high art and traditional storytelling; retell myth with contemporary lenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews describe The Perfect Nine as 'a quest novel-in-verse that explores folklore, myth and allegory' and as a work that 'refuses distinctions between "high art" and traditional storytelling', using a feminist and pan‑African lens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance implied by the page: creative work can (and in Ngũgĩ's case should) fuse formal literary ambition with traditional/oral narrative forms, reimagining origin stories and myths through contemporary thematic lenses (e.g., feminist, pan‑African) to produce meaningful, culturally rooted art.

rubrics_metrics.name: A powerful novel speaks with compelling urgency and emotional resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ's reflection on George Lamming: 'a novel could be made to speak to me, could, with a compelling urgency, touch cords deep down in me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This articulates a qualitative standard for fiction: works should engage readers urgently and emotionally, reaching deep human concerns. It's presented as part of Ngũgĩ's aesthetic formation and an implicit criterion for evaluating the potency of novels.
